name: Basílica da Estrela
seoTitle: Basílica da Estrela by Tram 28E or Taxi from the Ship
tagline: A domed late-18th-century basilica on the tram 28E route in western Lisbon, with Queen Maria I's tomb and a Machado de Castro nativity scene.

description.short: The Basílica da Estrela is a domed church built in 1779–1790 for Queen Maria I, opposite the Jardim da Estrela in western Lisbon. Entry is free. It holds the queen's tomb and a nativity scene of around 500 cork and terracotta figures by Machado de Castro.
description.full:
The Basílica da Estrela is a large late-18th-century church in a residential part of western Lisbon, about 3.4 km from the ship and uphill most of the way. It is not a practical walk on a port day, so treat it as a stop on a tram 28E ride or a taxi trip, and combine it with the Jardim da Estrela across the road.

Getting there: tram 28E stops right outside. You can board westbound at Sé, about 13 minutes' walk from the terminal, but from mid-morning to late afternoon the trams often arrive full and you may have to let several pass. On a short call, a taxi (12–15 minutes) is the reliable option; you can then take the tram back east if it suits.

Inside, prioritise the view up into the dome, the grey, pink and yellow marble, and the tomb of Queen Maria I in the right transept. Nearby, in a separate room, is the nativity scene by Joaquim Machado de Castro and his workshop, with around 500 cork and terracotta figures; a small charge may apply. If you can manage stairs, the rooftop terrace lets you walk around the roof and look down into the church from the dome; it is reported to cost about €5, but times and prices are not published officially, so check at the entrance.

Timing: it is an active parish church, with Mass at 12:00 and 19:00 daily and also at 10:00 on Sundays and holy days. Avoid sightseeing during services. Some sources report a lunchtime closure, so mid-morning or mid-afternoon is the safest window. Cover shoulders and knees.

What to skip: if you have only a few hours in Lisbon, the Baixa, Alfama and the castle come first. Do not plan a special tram 28E trip around this church in peak season.

Context: Maria I built it to fulfil a vow for a male heir.
description.history: Maria I and her husband, Pedro III, vowed to build a church if they had a son and heir. Prince José was born in 1761, and work on the basilica and an attached Carmelite convent began in 1779, designed by architects of the Mafra school, Mateus Vicente de Oliveira and later Reinaldo Manuel dos Santos. José died of smallpox in 1788, two years before the church was finished in 1790. It was the first church in the world dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Maria I died in Brazil in 1816, where the court had moved during the French invasions; her remains were later brought back and placed here.
description.significance: The dome is a landmark of western Lisbon's skyline, and the church is a late example of the Mafra school moving towards neoclassicism. It holds the tomb of Maria I, Portugal's first reigning queen, and one of the country's best-known nativity scenes by Machado de Castro, the leading Portuguese sculptor of his time. As a working parish church, it is far calmer than the cathedral or Jerónimos.

directions.general: Located in Estrela neighborhood, directly opposite Estrela Garden (Jardim da Estrela), on a hill west of city center
directions.fromCruisePort: About 3.4 km west, roughly 50 minutes on foot with hills, so not a practical walk on a port day. Tram 28 stops outside the basilica (board at Sé, a 13-minute walk from the terminal), or take a taxi (about 12-15 minutes).
directions.publicTransport: Tram 28E stops directly in front (Estrela). Nearest metro: Rato (Yellow Line), about 10 minutes' walk.
directions.parking: Street parking around Praça da Estrela and nearby streets. Parking can be challenging to find.

distanceFromCruisePort.walkingTime: Not practical on foot (52 min walk)

openingTimes.currentStatus: Open daily as a parish church; official visiting hours are not published

seasonal.notes: Times reported by several guides, not by the parish; some report a closure around 13:00–15:00. Mass daily at 12:00 and 19:00, plus 10:00 on Sundays and holy days.
Not officially published; confirm at the entrance. Reached by stairs only.

closedDates: Sightseeing restricted during Mass and special services

admissionPrices.notes: Free entry to the basilica. The rooftop terrace is reported to cost about €5 and the nativity scene may carry a small separate charge; neither price is published officially, so check on arrival.

visitingInformation.averageVisitDuration: 30–45 minutes, plus about 20 minutes for the terrace
visitingInformation.bestTimeToVisit: Mid-morning (10:00–11:45) or mid-afternoon, avoiding the 12:00 and 19:00 Masses and a possible lunchtime closure.
busyPeriods: Religious holidays and the Christmas season, when the nativity scene draws visitors
visitingInformation.adviceForVisitors: Cover shoulders and knees and keep quiet during services. Take a taxi if time is short: tram 28E is often full from mid-morning. Cross the road to the Jardim da Estrela for a shaded break.

cruisePassengerInfo.timeNeededFromPort: 2–2.5 hours by taxi; 3 hours or more if you rely on tram 28E
cruisePassengerInfo.accessibility: Too far and hilly to walk from the terminal; take a taxi or tram 28E. There are steps at the entrance, and the rooftop terrace is reached by stairs only.

tips: It is too far and hilly to walk from the ship (about 3.4 km); take a taxi (12–15 minutes) or tram 28E, which stops outside.
Board tram 28E westbound at Sé, 13 minutes' walk from the terminal; from mid-morning trams often arrive full, so allow extra time or take a taxi.
Entry is free. The rooftop terrace is reported at about €5, but times and prices are not published officially; ask at the entrance.
Mass is at 12:00 and 19:00 daily, plus 10:00 on Sundays and holy days; plan your visit around these times.
Find the Machado de Castro nativity scene, around 500 cork and terracotta figures, in a room near Queen Maria I's tomb; a small charge may apply.

Cross to the Jardim da Estrela opposite for a shaded break before heading back.

highlights: White dome, a landmark of western Lisbon's skyline
Twin bell towers and a façade with statues by Machado de Castro and his pupils
Interior of grey, pink and yellow marble
Tomb of Queen Maria I in the right transept
Nativity scene of around 500 cork and terracotta figures by Machado de Castro
Rooftop terrace with a walk around the dome (fee, stairs only)
Tram 28E stop and the Jardim da Estrela outside

accessibility.mobilityNotes: Steps at the entrance; the main floor is level once inside. The rooftop terrace is reached by stairs only.
